At first, I tried to think of it as an insurance premium, trying to calculate a hedge. But then I started to second-guess and that I was overthinking the rules, so I just kind of did a quick little math guess on a few.

For the random box task, I focused a lot on the probabilities of hitting the best boxes (that paid a lot or lost little/nothing) and tried to weigh the amount of money I'd pay accordingly, factoring in potential gains. I thought about hedging by paying a higher amount in order to have a higher likelihood of securing a gain, even if it was a smaller one. For example, in one of the green money-earning tasks, if there 90 boxes that paid big and 10 that paid nothing, I thought about wagering a higher amount in order to get at least a little extra, since it was very likely I'd hit one of the 90 good boxes and the randomly selected wager/payment amount could be less than the maximum I provided. For the much lower probability ones, e.g. 90 boxes that are empty and 10 that paid big, I was much less interested in trying to hit the big gains and was more worried about keeping my initial money. The reverse was also true for the red negative tasks, and if there were, say, 90 boxes with a big loss, I was willing to pay a bigger premium to hedge against said big loss.

For the average box task, once I got the hang of it, I realized that because you can calculate what the average amount will be (you know exactly what you'll get), you can set your maximums accordingly. I acted with this in mind, mostly wagering with the idea of hedging and securing at least small gains and losses. One thing I did similarly to the random box task is that I acted with the knowledge that the randomly selected amount may be lower than the maximum I offered, so this would increase my gains on the green positive tasks and reduce the premium I had to pay to hedge against losses on the red negative tasks.
